item.title: Scalable photonic quantum computer provides new insights into the fundamentals that shape its performance
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights Germany’s first scalable photonic quantum processor—a Gaussian boson sampler that lets researchers probe which quantum resources actually drive performance, a question that has lingered since early photonic experiments. By moving beyond small‑scale demonstrations toward a modular architecture, the work bridges the gap between proof‑of‑principle sampling and fault‑tolerant photonic computing, complementing recent advances in silicon‑photonics chips and error‑mitigation techniques. The insights could steer hardware design choices for future photonic processors targeting chemistry, materials science, and cryptographic applications, while reminding readers that scaling still hinges on loss reduction and efficient photon generation.

Photonics-based quantum computers open up new possibilities for investigating highly complex problems in mathematics and have the potential to revolutionize fields ranging from energy and chemical research to secure communications. By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. At Paderborn University, researchers are now investigating a fundamental question using Germany's first scalable photonic quantum computer, a 'Gaussian boson sampler': which quantum resources are most important for the performance of these devices?

item.title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a fully integrated multilayer ion‑trap chip that generates a spatial RF magnetic‑field gradient, enabling the preparation, coherent control and selective readout of microwave‑dressed hyperfine qubits in $^{171}$Yb⁺. By embedding the resonator on‑chip, the researchers achieve individual addressing and tunable coupling between dressed‑state qubits without relying on tightly focused laser beams, a step that could simplify scaling to larger ion arrays and reduce magnetic‑field noise. The work builds on recent advances in microwave‑driven gates and shows how hardware‑level engineering of RF fields can improve coherence and gate flexibility, although the demonstrations so far are limited to two‑ion crystals.

We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances. We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.

item.title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a first‑quantised phase‑estimation approach, built on a sum‑of‑squares Hamiltonian representation and spectral‑gap amplification, can slash the logical gate count needed for realistic molecular simulations by up to an order of magnitude compared with the best second‑quantised methods. By exploiting the low‑filling regime—where each electron is encoded in only logarithmically many qubits—the authors demonstrate a concrete pathway to chemistry calculations on hardware that will initially have far fewer than the thousands of logical qubits traditionally assumed necessary. The results suggest that near‑term error‑corrected devices could tackle chemically relevant systems sooner, though full fault‑tolerant overheads and state‑preparation costs still need careful assessment.

Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

item.title: Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a quantum‑enhanced wavelet transform can estimate the Hurst exponent of fractional Brownian motion with root‑N statistical efficiency, a scaling that matches classical optimal estimators while exploiting quantum amplitude‑estimation primitives. By eliminating the endpoint jump through a one‑qubit mirror extension and compiling the transform from paraunitary filter banks, the authors achieve up to an order‑of‑magnitude reduction in RMSE for modest‑size data (512 points), highlighting a concrete advantage for quantum‑enabled signal‑processing and sensing tasks. The work bridges recent advances in quantum wavelet circuits with practical time‑series analysis, though its impact will depend on scaling the method to larger datasets and integrating it into near‑term hardware platforms.

How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $ε$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cramér--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.0451$ for direct measurement and $0.0295$ with exact shares.

item.title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces Soft‑MoQE, a mixture‑of‑experts framework that replaces costly variational training with a classical gating network that selects and combines fixed quantum feature maps, thereby sidestepping barren‑plateau issues and dramatically lowering quantum resource demands. By achieving performance on MNIST‑derived tasks comparable to trainable quantum neural networks while using orders of magnitude less quantum optimization, it demonstrates a practical route for near‑term hybrid QML on noisy hardware. The approach builds on recent trends toward static quantum embeddings and adaptive classical routing, suggesting that smarter use of existing circuits can unlock useful quantum advantage without deep parameter tuning. Readers should note that the benchmarks rely on PCA‑reduced data, so further validation on larger, less preprocessed datasets will be needed to confirm scalability.

Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

item.title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article formalizes “reaction depth,” a key bottleneck that arises when quantum processors must pause for classical feed‑forward decisions, and shows how it can be decoupled from the underlying circuit depth. By proving that coherent Boolean arithmetic can be executed with both constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth using LDPC‑friendly Pauli‑product measurements and Toffoli states, the work offers a pathway to dramatically lower latency in fault‑tolerant algorithms such as Shor’s or large‑scale optimization routines. The trade‑off—exponential space overhead and reliance on “dirty” ancilla qubits—means the technique is most attractive for architectures that can afford abundant qubits but are constrained by classical‑quantum communication delays.

Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

item.title: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC$^{(1)}$ in 1D
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first rigorously proven polynomial‑time classical algorithm for estimating first‑order out‑of‑time‑order correlators in one‑dimensional Haar‑random brickwork circuits, closing a long‑standing gap between empirical evidence of tractability and formal guarantees. By introducing “window propagation,” the authors show that even deep random circuits—up to hundreds of qubits—can be simulated with inverse‑polynomial error, which tempers expectations that OTOC measurement alone will furnish near‑term quantum advantage. The result also provides a concrete benchmark for future hardness proofs and highlights that higher‑order OTOCs in two dimensions remain the more promising frontier for demonstrating genuine quantum supremacy.

Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. Even for first-order OTOCs, where growing evidence suggests classical tractability, no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has been established to date. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to $512$ qubits for Clifford circuits with $768$ $T$-gates and up to $22$ qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.

item.title: Instanton tunnelling as a verifiable benchmark for digital quantum simulation: circuit structure, classical simulability and hardware reproducibility
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a rare “exact‑by‑construction” benchmark for digital quantum simulators by exploiting instanton tunnelling in a quartic double‑well, allowing every intermediate result to be compared against an analytically known answer. By encoding the lattice with a single‑excitation (unary) mapping, the authors prove that the circuit’s entanglement stays bounded (Schmidt rank ≤ 4), which makes matrix‑product‑state simulations tractable even up to 48 sites and reveals a clear N⁻² scaling of the admissible Trotter step. Demonstrating reproducible tunnelling splittings on two superconducting processors, the work provides a practical yardstick for assessing hardware fidelity and error drift in near‑term devices while highlighting that larger lattices will still demand careful Trotter optimisation.

We use instanton-mediated tunnelling in the quartic double well as a benchmark for digital quantum simulation that is checkable against an exact answer at every step. The instanton enters through the classical analysis; the hardware tests the dynamics of the lattice model. A unary (single-excitation) encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits, with the single-excitation dynamics as a reference that remains classically cheap at any N. For a second-order Trotter circuit with adjacent, equal-angle XX/YY pairs on each bond, we prove that the Schmidt rank across any cut is at most four at every gate boundary and at most two after each pair, independently of N. Matrix-product-state simulations of this gate list reproduce the exact splitting up to N = 48. For this bond-wise formula the admissible Trotter step shrinks roughly as N^-2, so one tunnelling period costs about N^3.3 two-qubit gates; a kinetic/potential splitting keeps the step near 0.065 up to N=128, so this scaling belongs to splitting the kinetic term bond by bond. At a coarser, separately bounded step we measure the full transfer at N=8 on two superconducting processors, recovering the lattice splitting to a few percent and its dependence on the barrier height, which at this resolution is set by the lattice rather than by the instanton. Over 9 repetitions, runs taken minutes apart agree to shot noise, while runs hours to weeks apart differ by up to 6.1%, also on a fixed set of qubits; with sessions as the sampling unit, the processors differ in the damping, while a difference in the splitting is not established. Normalising by the measured single-excitation population extends the usable depth about 4-fold but does not improve the splitting. A Gaussian start state, which needs no diagonalisation, reproduces the splitting of the eigenvector-based start to within 1.6 percentage points.

item.title: No-Go Theorems for Ordered Universal Entanglement Purification
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article proves a strong no‑go theorem: even when noisy Bell pairs are known only by their fidelity ordering, any separable (and thus LOCC) success map that never reduces the best input fidelity must leave that fidelity unchanged, ruling out nontrivial universal purification for finite batches. The result sharpens earlier partial impossibility proofs and tells designers of quantum‑network repeaters that “one‑size‑fits‑all” entanglement‑purification stages cannot rely solely on ordering information—more detailed state knowledge or adaptive protocols remain essential. Consequently, researchers must focus on tailored or probabilistic purification schemes rather than expecting a universal boost from ordered ensembles, a reality that will shape near‑term hardware architectures with limited memory and heterogeneous link qualities.

Entanglement purification is a fundamental tool for obtaining high-fidelity entangled states used in various quantum technologies. It aims to increase the fidelity of noisy shared entangled states with a fixed maximally entangled state through LOCC. In distributed quantum systems, such as networks employing quantum repeaters, limited memory, probabilistic entanglement generation, and unequal storage times can leave a finite collection of nonidentical pairs. Their states may remain incompletely characterized even when calibrated preparation and storage records establish their fidelity ordering. Recent work has investigated whether fidelity ordering permits nontrivial universal purification. A nontrivial universal $n$-to-1 protocol must, conditioned on success, never lower the highest input fidelity and strictly increase it for at least one allowed joint input. Although no-go results have been established for a restricted class of LOCC protocols, the corresponding question for general LOCC has remained unresolved. Here, we study ordered universal purification under separable operations. Specifically, for every fixed finite $n\ge2$, we prove that when independently prepared two-qubit pairs range over the full family of states above a fixed fidelity threshold $0\le F_*<1$, any separable success map that never lowers the highest input fidelity on the allowed ordered inputs must preserve that fidelity exactly whenever it succeeds. This excludes nontrivial universal LOCC purification even for arbitrarily high input fidelities, without imposing a positive lower bound on success probability. ...

item.title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a hybrid quantum‑classical scheme that pushes the frontier of real‑time simulations for strongly correlated electrons by offloading the most demanding impurity dynamics onto a quantum processor while handling the lattice quasiparticles classically. By embedding ghost orbitals and using adaptive variational circuits, the authors demonstrate near‑exact agreement with dynamical mean‑field theory on modest qubit counts, showing that even today’s noisy hardware can capture nontrivial nonequilibrium physics beyond conventional Gutzwiller approximations. The work therefore provides a concrete pathway for leveraging NISQ devices to tackle long‑standing many‑body problems in materials science, albeit still limited by circuit depth and noise mitigation requirements.

Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

item.title: On a local hidden-variable model for postselected EPR correlations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a purely classical, locally‑causal model can mimic Bell‑type violations when the detector’s response is made dependent on measurement settings and postselection is applied, highlighting how subtle detection‑efficiency loopholes can masquerade as quantum correlations. By quantifying the parameter regimes where such a sigmoid‑threshold mechanism reproduces the CHSH and Eberhard statistics for nonmaximally entangled states, it underscores why recent loophole‑free Bell tests that enforce fair sampling are essential for trustworthy device‑independent protocols. The work also provides a useful benchmark for simulators of quantum hardware, reminding researchers that any claim of nonlocality must be vetted against sophisticated local‑hidden‑variable constructions that exploit adaptive thresholds.

A theoretical and numerical analysis of a Bell-type experiment is presented, where linear polarization measurements on nonmaximally entangled two-qubit states are modeled through a sigmoid-based threshold mechanism that violates the fair-sampling assumption required by the CHSH inequality. Numerical simulations characterize how closely this local construction can reproduce quantum-like correlations in the postselected detected sample, for both the |Phi_r> and |Psi_r> states over a range of entanglement parameters. For the tested configurations, the model produces CHSH-type violations only in the postselected detected sample through a setting-dependent detection mechanism, operating outside the assumptions of both the CHSH inequality and Mermin's 82.8% efficiency bound. The model is not in conflict with loophole-free Bell experiments, which specifically close the detection loophole exploited here. The CH--Eberhard analysis in the one-detector-per-side configuration yields J < 0 throughout the full range of entanglement parameters, as required for a strictly local model. The model is further extended with a local adaptive-threshold mechanism implementing one-sided memory. A paired comparison shows that this specific memory rule produces a systematic and reproducible shift in the CH--Eberhard parameter J relative to the fixed-threshold model, while leaving the CH--Eberhard analysis qualitatively unchanged under the tested conditions. The results characterize how a local, setting-dependent postselection mechanism shapes Bell-test statistics across a range of entanglement parameters, within the specific configurations and threshold rules tested.

The protocol introduced by C. H. Bennett, G. Brassard and N. D. Mermin in 1992 (BBM92) is one of the most important and widely adopted quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. As with any other QKD protocol, its practical security depends on satisfying the assumptions underlying its theoretical security proofs. Here, we examine two common implementations of BBM92: a conventional passive receiver and a time-multiplexed configuration that halves the number of detectors. We characterise the passive polarisation analysers common to both architectures and present experimental results obtained with the time-multiplexed receiver, employing a continuous-wave (CW) pumped spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source of polarisation-entangled photon pairs and threshold detectors. We investigate the challenges encountered during post-processing when attempting to satisfy the requirements of existing security proofs and discuss the gap between theoretical security assumptions and the extraction of a provably secure cryptographic key.

item.title: Bound entanglement as a trigonometric moment problem
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article translates the notoriously opaque problem of PPT‑bound entanglement into a tractable trigonometric moment framework, allowing the authors to pinpoint exactly which three‑qubit bound‑entangled states lie in a natural family of spin‑coherent mixtures and to derive closed‑form noise‑robustness thresholds. By linking separability to the positivity of a multi‑level Toeplitz matrix, it supplies a new set of invariants that complement recent classification efforts for low‑rank entangled states and could streamline the design of experimental tests for bound entanglement. The results sharpen our theoretical toolbox for detecting and quantifying PPT entanglement, although their immediate hardware impact remains indirect until such states can be reliably prepared in laboratory qubit arrays.

Entangled states that are positive under partial transposition (PPT) are the main obstruction to a simple description of entanglement. We study three basic questions about them within a class of multiqubit states, the mixtures, with real but possibly negative weights, of products of equatorial spin coherent states of several groups of qubits: which PPT entangled states belong to the class, how robust their entanglement is to white noise, and how small their rank can be. In this class each question becomes a question about a truncated trigonometric moment problem. Every such state is PPT across every bipartition, and it is fully separable exactly when an associated multi-level Toeplitz matrix is the moment matrix of a positive measure on the torus. We answer the three questions exactly in the following cases. For three qubits, every rank-four PPT entangled state with nonzero Lorentz invariant belongs to the class after invertible local operators, which proves a working hypothesis of Garberg, Irgens and Myrheim and yields a complete set of invariants for this seven-dimensional family; among the states with vanishing invariant, exactly a one-parameter family belongs to it. For every three-qubit state built from an unextendible product basis, the white-noise threshold for full separability is $λ^*=1-2/(1+\sqrt{1+s})$ with a local-unitary invariant $s\in(0,1]$, and $λ^*=3-2\sqrt2$ for the Shifts basis; a witness in closed form detects every entangled state of this family with eight local Pauli settings. For two groups of qubits we construct extremal states of minimal rank, and for three groups we determine the minimal rank of entanglement within the class in several configurations.

item.title: Doppler effect on dual-downlink time-bin quantum key distribution and a proposed ephemeris-assisted witness-field correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a key obstacle for space‑based time‑bin QKD—tiny Doppler‑induced phase shifts that can cripple the entangled‑photon correlations needed for secure keys. By showing that each ground station can locally reconstruct and pre‑compensate its own Doppler phase using an ephemeris‑driven witness field, the authors provide a practical feed‑forward solution that avoids real‑time quantum communication between stations. We present a spectral-temporal framework for time-bin-entangled photon pairs generated onboard a satellite via Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion (SPDC) and distributed to two Optical Ground Stations (OGSs) over independent downlinks with distinct Doppler shifts. Each OGS is equipped with an Unbalanced Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (UMZI) used to perform Bennett-Brassard-Mermin 1992 (BBM92) entangled-photon QKD. In a simulated Low Earth Orbit (LEO) pass with matched 400 ps analyzer delays, the received time-bin separation changes by at most 8.8 fs per link, while the combined carrier phase shifts by about 38 rad, which primarily degrades phase-basis correlations. After zero-Doppler calibration, this phase separates into independent signal-and idler-link contributions, allowing each station to correct its link Doppler phase shift locally, without real-time phase exchange between the stations. In a noise-free model, a 1 Hz sample-and-hold correction rate keeps the phase-basis Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) below 2% and retains 93% of the ideal asymptotic key yield. After 18 accumulated passes, the corrected finite secret key reaches 95% of its ideal length, whereas relabeling the parity from the ephemeris without optical correction reaches only about 8%.

item.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers a concrete microarchitectural solution—QuFrame—that finally bridges the gap between theoretical Pauli‑frame tracking and the sub‑microsecond control loops required for fault‑tolerant universal quantum computation. By decoupling instruction execution from real‑time frame updates and providing lock‑free, per‑qubit engines plus an on‑chip fallback decoder that resolves in 144 ns, QuFrame builds on recent advances in surface‑code decoding and pushes the QEC cycle time down to the 1 µs regime needed for magic‑state injection. If integrated into scalable control stacks, this approach could make continuous error correction practical for larger processors, though its real‑world performance will still depend on tight hardware–software co‑design and validation on actual quantum devices.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

item.title: Quantifying extractable imaginarity with qubit triangles
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a geometric “qubit‑triangle” framework that turns the abstract notion of imaginarity into a concrete, convex monotone measure, linking it directly to the Bures χ² divergence and quantum Fisher information. By showing how real‑only operations can extract or fail to extract imaginarity—sometimes even forbidding deterministic conversion between states with identical robustness—it clarifies a resource limitation that will matter for hardware platforms constrained to real gate sets or phase‑restricted control. The results give practitioners a computable tool for assessing when complex amplitudes are truly needed, guiding both algorithm design and the development of more expressive quantum processors.

Two qubit states with the same robustness of imaginarity can differ in the robustness attainable by real filtering on a successful outcome. We represent the input robustness $R$ and the largest conditional robustness $κ$ by the base of a right triangle and the slope of its hypotenuse, respectively. Twice the area, $R^2κ$, defines a faithful, convex measure that is monotone on average under real instruments. In arbitrary finite dimensions, maximizing the mean normalized area of the extracted qubits gives the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension of the qubit measure. We derive computable bounds on this area by determining the maximum mean squared robustness of the output qubits. This maximum equals the Bures quantum $χ^2$ divergence between the input and its real part. A projection onto orthogonal real subspaces attains the maximum and, when its outcome is retained, preserves the quantum Fisher information at the midpoint of a mixture of the input and its complex conjugate. We obtain exact areas for states with commuting real and imaginary parts and for pure states mixed with white noise. Two eight-dimensional states have identical $R$, $κ$, and optimal mean squared robustness, yet their different areas rule out deterministic conversion by real operations in one direction.

We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. item.title: Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article uncovers a subtle “gradient blindness” that can cripple adaptive architecture searches for IQP Born machines, showing that the choice of seed circuit determines which higher‑order gates ever receive a nonzero training signal. By proving that only generators formed from an odd number of existing linearly independent terms have observable gradients, the authors demonstrate that seeding with one‑qubit gates plus Chow‑Liu tree edges restores full expressivity while shrinking parameter counts to roughly 10 % of dense models—even on 484‑qubit instances. Instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines learn a probability distribution from data with a circuit of commuting gates that a classical computer trains at hundreds of qubits. Adaptive algorithms grow a sparse circuit from a small seed by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient. Such algorithms never add a candidate whose gradient vanishes, so the choice of seed decides which circuits they can reach. Here we show that a candidate gate has a nonzero gradient for some angles of the circuit exactly when its generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. The common seed of one-qubit gates therefore never adds a gate on an even number of qubits, which exact gradients on 12 qubits confirm. A seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree sees every candidate, and its circuits match the full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits with 10 to 13 percent of their parameters. At 484 qubits, a heredity pool keeps the search over higher-order gates feasible, and the circuits grown from this seed reach a lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit with 6 percent of its parameters, although the higher-order gates add no gain.

The resulting circuit has depth dominated solely by that of the input oracle and independent of the number of matrices k, at the cost of a qubit count scaling as Θ(k)-a trade-off between circuit depth and circuit size. Both reduce the target problem to sums of multivariate traces, thereby avoiding the construction of matrix polynomial transformations and achieving two levels of parallelism. For certain matrix classes, the resulting algorithms reduce circuit depth by a factor equal to the degree of the approximating polynomial. The shallow circuit depth and distributed implementation make our algorithms particularly suitable for near-term devices.

item.title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a concrete pathway for using early fault‑tolerant quantum computers to simulate nonlinear fluid flows by marrying sparse‑identified reduced‑order models with Walsh‑based Koopman‑von Neumann transport, showing that the per‑step gate count grows only polylogarithmically with spatial resolution. By providing realistic surface‑code resource estimates—about 560 k physical qubits and under two hours for a cylinder‑wake benchmark—it moves quantum simulation from abstract algorithmic proposals toward hardware‑compatible workloads. The work builds on recent advances in quantum PDE solvers and error‑mitigated experiments, suggesting that practical, high‑fidelity nonlinear dynamics could become one of the first near‑term applications where quantum advantage is measurable. However, the projected runtimes still depend on large qubit counts and efficient noise mitigation, so further hardware improvements will be needed before routine deployment.

Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

item.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first experimental teleportation of logical qubits using lattice‑surgery on a superconducting processor with 41 physical qubits, demonstrating that surface‑code patches can be merged and split while preserving encoded information. By showing how repeated stabilizer measurements restore fault tolerance and improve fidelity, it connects directly to recent efforts by Google, IBM and academic groups to build scalable error‑corrected architectures. The ability to move logical states without physically shuttling qubits paves the way for modular quantum processors, although the distance‑three code still leaves room for higher fidelities before full fault‑tolerant operation is achieved.

Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the fault‑tolerance advantage of logical encoding in fusion‑based photonic quantum computers can evaporate when realistic photon‑distinguishability errors are included, highlighting a hidden vulnerability of otherwise promising architectures. By contrasting all‑photonic and emitter‑assisted repeat‑until‑success schemes, the authors demonstrate that the choice of resource‑state generation method can be as decisive for error thresholds as the encoding itself—a nuance that recent photonic hardware roadmaps have largely overlooked. The findings urge experimental teams to prioritize indistinguishability control and to reassess performance projections that assume idealized resource states before scaling up FBQC platforms.

Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.

item.title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces PRISM, a compiler that postpones the choice of a logical‑gate’s physical realization until routing has identified a layout that can execute it, thereby turning a long‑standing phase‑ordering bottleneck into an optimization opportunity for dual‑rail cavity qubits. By keeping multiple loss‑admissible realizations open and selecting the most routing‑friendly one on the fly, PRISM cuts SWAP overhead by roughly 20–30 % and shrinks circuit depth by about 9 %, directly translating into fewer photon‑loss events and up to a 44 % reduction in required repeat attempts. The work demonstrates how hardware‑aware compilation can deliver tangible performance gains for photonic platforms, complementing recent efforts in error‑corrected logical encoding while still being scoped to dual‑rail architectures.

Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.

item.title: Variable-length MDI QKD under source imperfections and local randomization over horizontal links
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pushes measurement‑device‑independent QKD toward real‑world deployment by rigorously handling source flaws and finite‑size effects with a variable‑length security proof based on the marginal‑constrained entropy accumulation theorem. By showing that secret keys can be distilled from as few as 30 000 pulses—even over asymmetric, 80‑km horizontal links—the work bridges the gap between laboratory demonstrations and the longer distances required for commercial satellite constellations. The conic‑optimization framework also offers a practical tool for system designers to fine‑tune transmitter amplitudes and mitigate channel imbalance, though its performance still assumes ideal atmospheric conditions that must be addressed in future field trials.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides security guarantees that hold despite device imperfections and finite-size effects. We address these challenges in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, combining its intrinsic untrusted detection with an imperfection model for Alice's and Bob's sources via fidelity bounds. We establish variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT), estimating the relevant Rényi entropies through conic optimization. We evaluate our model under a horizontal channel link, reporting secret keys for blocks as small as n~3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions, and show that compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric configurations, enabling communication distances beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.
